title: Linked Lists
summary: Nodes connected by pointers: cheap to rearrange, expensive to index, and full of pointer-update traps.
keyPoints: Each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node; there is no index arithmetic.
Finding a node by position is O(n), but inserting or removing after a known node is O(1).
A dummy head removes special cases when the first node may change.
Fast and slow pointers find the middle and detect cycles without extra memory.
commonMistakes: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting `current.next` before saving it.
Forgetting to update the tail pointer or to set the last node's next to null.
Using a dummy node but forgetting to return `dummy.next` instead of `dummy`.
Dereferencing `current.next` without checking whether `current` is null.
interviewNotes: Draw the nodes and pointer arrows before coding. It is faster than debugging pointer changes later.
State which node each pointer references and the order of the assignments.
If the head can change, mention a dummy node as the way to avoid a special first case.

checkYourself.question: Why is reversing a linked list O(1) extra space?
checkYourself.answer: Only the next pointers are changed, one node at a time. No new nodes or arrays are needed.

checkYourself.question: How does a dummy node simplify deletion?
checkYourself.answer: It gives the first real node a predecessor, so the same pointer update works whether the removed node is first or later.

checkYourself.question: What happens if two pointers meet in a linked list?
checkYourself.answer: A cycle exists. The fast pointer cannot reach the end because it is looping.
